attempts.raw_response: The retreat was conducted in good order, our men falling back steadily, their bayonets still gleaming in the fading light. The enemy, wary of a trap, did not press their advantage. We marched through the night, exhausted but unbowed, leaving behind the dead and the burning waggons. The loss of the field was bitter, but the spirit of the army remained unbroken.

The retreat was conducted in good order, but the enemy, emboldened by their success, pressed hard upon our rear. The darkness of the night alone saved us from total destruction, as the pursuing cavalry could not distinguish friend from foe in the gloom. We marched through the hours until dawn, when we reached a small village, where we hoped to find some respite. But the inhabitants had fled, taking with them all provisions, and we were left to forage as best we could. The men, though exhausted and hungry, bore their hardships without murmur, their discipline unbroken. It was a bitter lesson, teaching us that even the bravest infantry cannot long withstand the shock of combined arms—cannon, horse, and steel—when unsupported by their own.

pair.human_continuation:
The agony of
the British, resident at Brussels, during the whole of this eventful
day, sets all language at defiance. No one thought of rest or food; but
every one who could get a telescope, flew to the ramparts to strain his
eyes, in vain attempts to discover what was passing. At length, some
soldiers in French uniforms were seen in the distance; and as the news
flew from mouth to mouth, it was soon magnified into a rumour that the
French were coming. Horror seized the English and their adherents, and
the hitherto concealed partizans of the French began openly to avow
themselves; tri-coloured ribbons grew suddenly into great request, and
cries of "Vive l'Empereur!" resounded through the air.
pair.prefix:
Cannon, lances, and swords, were opposed
to the English bayonet alone. Cavalry we had none on the first day, for
the horses had been sent to grass, and the men were scattered too widely
over the country, to be collected at such short notice. Under these
circumstances, victory was impossible; indeed, nothing but the stanch
bravery, and exact discipline of the men, prevented the foremost of our
infantry from being annihilated; and though the English maintained their
ground during the day, at night a retreat became necessary.
